title: Currency Derivatives
blurb: Currency markets, forwards, futures and options on USD-INR and other pairs, strategies, trading, settlement, regulation and tax.

units.title: Introduction to currency markets
units.overview: Exchange rates, quotes and how the foreign exchange market works.
facts: Exchange rate
An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another.
USD-INR at 83 means one dollar costs 83 rupees.
An exchange rate is the interest rate on currency loans.
Base and quote currency
In a pair quoted as A-B, A is the base currency and B is the quote currency, and the rate shows units of B per unit of A.
In USD-INR, the dollar is the base and the rupee is quoted.
In USD-INR, the rupee is the base currency.
Direct and indirect quote
A direct quote gives the home currency per unit of foreign currency; an indirect quote gives foreign currency per unit of home currency.
For an Indian dealer, 83 rupees per dollar is direct.
A direct quote shows foreign currency per rupee.
Bid and ask
The bid is the price at which a dealer buys the base currency and the ask is the price at which the dealer sells it, with the ask higher than the bid.
A dealer quotes 82.98-83.02.
The bid is higher than the ask.
Spread
The spread is the difference between ask and bid and is the dealer's margin and a measure of liquidity.
A narrow spread shows a liquid pair.
A wide spread signals high liquidity.
Appreciation and depreciation
A currency appreciates when it buys more foreign currency and depreciates when it buys less.
USD-INR rising from 82 to 84 means the rupee has depreciated.
A rising USD-INR means the rupee has strengthened.
Cross rate
A cross rate between two currencies is derived from their rates against a third, usually the dollar.
EUR-INR is computed from EUR-USD and USD-INR.
Cross rates are fixed by the central bank.
Spot market
In the spot market currencies are bought and sold for settlement in two working days.
A bank buys dollars for delivery after two days.
Spot trades are settled after one year.
Interbank market
The interbank market is where banks trade large amounts of currency among themselves and sets reference rates.
Banks quote to each other over electronic platforms.
The interbank market is only for retail customers.
Market participants
Participants include banks, corporates, exporters, importers, investors, speculators and central banks.
An importer buys dollars to pay a foreign supplier.
Only banks take part in currency markets.
Hedgers and speculators
Hedgers use derivatives to reduce existing currency risk; speculators take risk hoping to profit from price moves.
An exporter sells dollars forward to lock in a rate.
Hedgers aim to profit from price moves.
Arbitrageurs
Arbitrageurs exploit price differences in the same or related instruments across markets to earn low-risk profit.
A trader buys dollars on one venue and sells on another at a higher price.
Arbitrageurs take large directional bets.
Exchange rate regimes
Regimes range from fixed to floating; India follows a managed float where the central bank may intervene to curb volatility.
The RBI sells dollars to steady the rupee.
India has a rigidly fixed rate.
Drivers of exchange rates
Rates move with interest rate differentials, inflation, trade and capital flows, growth and sentiment.
Heavy foreign portfolio inflows strengthen the rupee.
Exchange rates depend only on exports.
Purchasing power parity
PPP says exchange rates adjust so that price levels are equal across countries, so higher inflation tends to weaken a currency.
A country with high inflation sees its currency weaken over time.
PPP says high inflation strengthens the currency.
Foreign exchange reserves
Reserves are foreign currency assets held by the central bank to manage the exchange rate and meet external obligations.
The RBI uses reserves to curb sharp falls.
Reserves are held by commercial banks only.
Balance of payments
The balance of payments records a country's transactions with the rest of the world and is an important driver of currency demand.
A large current account deficit puts pressure on the currency.
The balance of payments records only government spending.

units.title: Foreign exchange derivatives
units.overview: Forwards, swaps and the basics of pricing and hedging.
facts: Forward contract
A forward contract is a customised agreement to buy or sell a currency at a fixed rate on a future date, traded over the counter.
An importer books dollars for delivery in three months.
A forward contract is traded on an exchange with standard terms.
Forward premium and discount
A currency trades at a forward premium if the forward rate is above spot and at a discount if below.
With rupee interest rates above dollar rates, USD-INR forwards trade at a premium.
A forward premium means the forward is below spot.
Interest rate parity
Interest rate parity links the forward rate to spot and the interest rate differential, so the currency with higher interest rate trades at a forward discount.
The forward rate reflects the difference in rupee and dollar interest rates.
Forward rates are independent of interest rates.
Forward rate formula
Forward rate is approximately spot x (1 + rupee rate x t) / (1 + dollar rate x t).
Spot 83 with a higher rupee rate gives a forward above 83.
Forward rate equals spot always.
Currency swap
A currency swap exchanges principal and interest in one currency for another over a period.
Two firms swap loans in different currencies.
A swap is an exchange-traded futures contract.
Non-deliverable forward
An NDF is settled in cash in a convertible currency based on the difference between the contract rate and a fixing rate, with no delivery of the restricted currency.
Offshore parties trade rupee NDFs settled in dollars.
An NDF requires physical delivery.
OTC versus exchange traded
OTC contracts are customised and carry counterparty risk, while exchange-traded contracts are standardised and guaranteed by the clearing corporation.
A futures trade is guaranteed by the clearing corporation.
OTC contracts are guaranteed by the exchange.
Hedging with forwards
An exporter expecting dollars sells them forward to fix the rupee amount, removing the risk of rupee appreciation.
An exporter locks in a rate for payment due in six months.
Hedging removes all possible gains and costs.
Exposure types
Transaction, translation and economic exposure describe how currency changes affect cash flows, balance sheets and long-term value.
A firm with dollar debt faces transaction exposure.
Exposure only arises for exporters.
Currency options OTC
Banks also offer OTC currency options that are customised for corporates.
A corporate buys a tailored dollar call from a bank.
OTC options are always exchange guaranteed.

units.title: Exchange traded currency futures
units.overview: The core of the exam. Contract specifications, pricing, profit and loss, and hedging with futures.
visuals: Last working day of the month, two working days before
Profit = (Selling price - Buying price) x Lot size x Number of lots
facts: Currency futures
A currency future is a standardised exchange-traded contract to buy or sell a currency pair at a fixed price on a future date.
An investor buys USD-INR futures to bet on rupee depreciation.
A currency future is a customised OTC contract.
Contract size
The contract size of USD-INR futures is 1,000 US dollars per lot.
One lot represents $1,000.
The standard lot is $100,000.
Tick size and value
The tick is 0.0025 rupee, so one tick on a lot of 1,000 dollars is worth ₹2.50.
A move of 10 ticks equals ₹25 per lot.
The tick size is one rupee.
Quotation
Futures on USD-INR are quoted in rupees per dollar.
A price of 83.2500 means ₹83.25 per dollar.
The quote shows dollars per rupee.
Expiry and cycle
Contracts expire on the last working day of the month, with 12 monthly contracts available.
A contract for next month is available to trade.
Contracts expire on the first working day.
Cash settlement
Currency futures are settled in cash in rupees; there is no delivery of foreign currency.
At expiry, gains or losses are paid in rupees.
Physical dollars are delivered on expiry.
Final settlement price
The final settlement price is the RBI reference rate on the expiry day, used to settle open positions.
Open positions settle at the RBI reference rate.
The final price is the previous day's close.
Long and short futures
A long futures position gains if the currency pair rises, and a short position gains if it falls.
A buyer of USD-INR futures gains if the dollar rises against the rupee.
A long position gains when the price falls.
Futures profit and loss
Profit or loss equals the price change multiplied by the lot size and number of lots.
Buying at 83.00 and selling at 83.20 on one lot gives ₹200.
Profit is the price change multiplied by the margin.
Daily mark-to-market
Positions are marked to market each day, with gains credited and losses debited to the margin account.
A client whose position has fallen sees her margin reduced that evening.
Profit or loss arises only at expiry.
Cost of carry
The futures price is based on spot plus the cost of carry, which reflects the interest rate differential.
With higher rupee rates, the futures trade above spot.
Futures prices are unrelated to spot.
Basis
Basis is the difference between spot and futures price, which narrows to zero as expiry nears.
Futures converge to spot at expiry.
The basis widens at expiry.
Convergence
As expiry approaches, the futures price converges to the spot price.
The gap between spot and futures shrinks daily.
Futures diverge from spot near expiry.
Hedging with futures
A hedger takes a position in futures opposite to the exposure; an importer with dollar payables buys futures, and an exporter sells.
An importer buys USD-INR futures to lock in cost.
An importer hedges by selling dollar futures.
Speculation
Speculators take positions in futures to profit from price moves, using leverage through margin.
A trader buys a lot expecting the dollar to strengthen.
Speculators remove risk from the market.
Spread trading
A calendar spread involves buying one expiry and selling another, profiting from changes in the price gap.
A trader buys the near month and sells the far month.
A spread involves two different currency pairs only.
Open interest
Open interest is the total number of outstanding contracts not yet closed or settled.
Open interest rises when new positions are created.
Open interest is the number of trades in a day.
Leverage
Futures allow control of a large value with a small margin, magnifying gains and losses.
Margin of 3% allows exposure of about 33 times.
Leverage reduces risk.
Other pairs
Exchanges also offer futures on EUR-INR, GBP-INR and JPY-INR and cross-currency pairs.
A trader takes a view on the euro against the rupee.
Only USD-INR futures exist.
Contract value
The value of a contract is price multiplied by lot size.
At 83.00, one lot has a value of ₹83,000.
The contract value equals the margin.
Hedge ratio
The hedge ratio is the number of futures contracts required to cover an exposure, found by dividing the exposure by the lot size.
A $50,000 exposure needs 50 lots of $1,000.
A $50,000 exposure needs one lot.
Position limits
Exchanges and SEBI set limits on positions to prevent excessive speculation, with higher limits for hedgers under conditions.
A trader's position cannot exceed the stated cap.
There are no limits on positions.
Rolling over
Rolling over means closing a near-month position and opening a similar one in a later month to maintain exposure.
A hedger rolls her short position into next month.
Rolling over means taking delivery.
Futures versus forwards
Futures are standardised, exchange traded, daily settled and guaranteed by the clearing corporation, while forwards are customised and carry counterparty risk.
Futures are marked to market daily, forwards are not.
Forwards are settled daily.

units.title: Exchange traded currency options
units.overview: Option terminology, payoffs, premium, and factors affecting option value.
visuals: Call: Strike + Premium. Put: Strike - Premium.
facts: Currency option
A currency option gives the buyer the right but not the obligation to buy or sell a currency at a fixed rate on or before a date.
A buyer pays a premium for the right to buy dollars at 83.
An option obliges both parties to trade.
Call option
A call gives the right to buy the underlying at the strike price.
The holder of a USD call gains if the dollar rises above the strike.
A call gives the right to sell.
Put option
A put gives the right to sell the underlying at the strike price.
The holder of a USD put gains if the dollar falls below the strike.
A put gives the right to buy.
Strike price
The strike price is the fixed rate at which the option can be exercised.
A call with a strike of 83.00 allows buying dollars at 83.
The strike is the premium paid.
Premium
The premium is the price paid by the buyer to the seller of the option, and is the buyer's maximum loss.
The buyer pays ₹0.50 per dollar.
The premium is paid at expiry only if exercised.
Option buyer and writer
The buyer pays the premium and has the right; the writer receives the premium and has the obligation if the buyer exercises.
A writer must deliver if the buyer exercises.
The buyer has an obligation to deliver.
European style
Exchange traded currency options in India are European style and can be exercised only on expiry.
The holder cannot exercise before the expiry day.
They can be exercised any time before expiry.
Cash settlement of options
Options are settled in cash in rupees, with the in-the-money amount paid at expiry.
A call with strike 83 and final price 84 pays ₹1 per dollar.
Options are settled by physical delivery.
In, at and out of the money
A call is in the money if spot is above strike; a put is in the money if spot is below strike; at the money if equal.
A put with strike 83 when spot is 82 is in the money.
A call is in the money if spot is below strike.
Intrinsic value
Intrinsic value is the in-the-money amount, and is zero if the option is out of the money.
A call with strike 82 and spot 83 has intrinsic value of 1.
Intrinsic value can be negative.
Time value
Time value is the premium minus intrinsic value and declines to zero at expiry.
An at-the-money option has only time value.
Time value increases near expiry.
Long call payoff
A long call's payoff is the greater of zero and spot minus strike, less premium paid.
Strike 83, premium 0.40, spot 84 gives a net 0.60.
A long call can lose more than the premium.
Long put payoff
A long put's payoff is the greater of zero and strike minus spot, less premium paid.
Strike 83, premium 0.40, spot 82 gives a net 0.60.
A long put has unlimited loss.
Short call risk
A short call has limited profit equal to the premium received and unlimited potential loss.
A writer of a call faces rising losses as the currency climbs.
A short call has limited loss.
Short put risk
A short put has limited profit equal to the premium received and substantial loss if the price falls.
A writer of a put loses if the currency falls sharply.
A short put has unlimited profit.
Factors affecting premium
Option premium depends on spot, strike, time to expiry, volatility and interest rate differentials.
Higher volatility raises both call and put premiums.
Volatility does not affect premium.
Volatility and premium
Greater expected volatility increases the chance of large moves and hence raises option premiums.
A calm market leads to cheaper options.
Falling volatility raises premiums.
Delta
Delta measures the change in option price for a unit change in the underlying; a call has positive delta and a put negative.
A delta of 0.5 means the option moves half as much as the currency.
Delta measures time decay.
Gamma
Gamma measures the rate of change of delta as the underlying moves.
A high gamma means delta changes quickly.
Gamma measures the effect of interest rates.
Theta
Theta measures the loss in option value as time passes, which hurts option buyers and helps sellers.
An option loses value each day, all else being equal.
Theta measures sensitivity to volatility.
Vega
Vega measures the change in option price for a change in volatility.
A rise in volatility lifts the option's price.
Vega measures the change with time.
Rho
Rho measures the sensitivity of option price to changes in interest rates.
A change in rate differential changes option value slightly.
Rho measures sensitivity to volatility.
Put-call parity
Put-call parity links the prices of a call and put with the same strike and expiry to the forward price.
A violation allows arbitrage.
Put and call prices are independent.
Hedging with options
Options let a hedger fix a worst-case rate while keeping the benefit of favourable moves, at the cost of the premium.
An importer buys a call to cap the price of dollars.
Options fix the rate completely like forwards.
Option contract specs
USD-INR options have a lot size of 1,000 dollars, a tick of 0.0025 and expiry on the last working day of the month with cash settlement.
One lot covers $1,000.
The lot size of options is $100,000.
Exercise and assignment
At expiry, in-the-money options are automatically exercised and writers are assigned by the clearing corporation.
A call with a profit is exercised without any instruction.
The holder must give a written exercise notice.

units.title: Strategies using exchange traded currency derivatives
units.overview: Combining futures and options to hedge or speculate.
visuals: Buy low call, sell high call
Buy high put, sell low put
Buy call and put at same strike
Buy OTM call and OTM put
facts: Bull call spread
A bull call spread buys a lower strike call and sells a higher strike call, limiting both cost and profit.
A trader expects a moderate rise in the dollar.
A bull call spread has unlimited profit.
Bear put spread
A bear put spread buys a higher strike put and sells a lower strike put to profit from a moderate fall.
A trader expects a moderate fall in the dollar.
A bear put spread profits when prices rise.
Long straddle
A long straddle buys a call and a put at the same strike and expiry and profits from a large move in either direction.
A trader expects a big move after an event but is unsure of direction.
A straddle profits when the market stays flat.
Short straddle
A short straddle sells a call and a put at the same strike, earning premium if the price stays near the strike, but with unlimited risk.
A trader expects a quiet market.
A short straddle has limited risk.
Long strangle
A strangle buys an out-of-the-money call and put, cheaper than a straddle but requiring a bigger move to profit.
A trader buys a 84 call and a 82 put.
A strangle is more expensive than a straddle.
Covered position
Combining an option with an underlying position, such as a short call against a long futures position, can enhance income but caps gains.
A holder of futures writes a call for premium.
A covered position removes all risk.
Protective put
Buying a put against a long exposure sets a floor on losses while keeping the upside.
An exporter holding dollars buys a put to protect against a fall.
A protective put caps the upside.
Maximum profit in a spread
In a bull call spread, maximum profit equals the difference in strikes less the net premium.
Strikes 83 and 84 with net premium 0.30 give a maximum profit of 0.70.
Maximum profit equals the net premium.
Hedging a payable
An importer with a dollar payable can buy futures or a call option to protect against dollar appreciation.
A firm buys a call to cap the cost of dollars.
An importer protects herself by selling dollar futures.
Hedging a receivable
An exporter with a dollar receivable can sell futures or buy a put to protect against dollar depreciation.
A firm buys a put to set a floor on rupee proceeds.
An exporter protects herself by buying dollar futures.
Choosing between futures and options
Futures lock the rate but remove favourable moves; options keep favourable moves at the cost of premium.
A hedger who wants upside buys an option.
Options cost nothing.
Margin and strategy risk
Short option legs require margin, and strategies must be assessed on net risk and capital needs.
A short straddle needs substantial margin.
Spread positions need no margin.

units.title: Trading mechanism
units.overview: How orders are placed and matched on the exchange.
facts: Trading hours
Currency derivatives trade on weekdays from 9:00 am to 5:00 pm, subject to exchange schedule.
A trader places an order at 4 pm.
Currency derivatives trade round the clock.
Order types
Exchanges allow market, limit and stop-loss orders, with validity such as day or immediate or cancel.
A trader places a limit order at a stated rate.
Only market orders are allowed.
Order matching
Orders are matched on price-time priority in an electronic order book.
The best priced and earliest order is filled first.
Orders are matched manually by the exchange.
Trading members and clients
Trading members execute for clients, and clients must be registered with unique client codes mapped to PAN.
A client trades through a registered broker.
Clients may trade directly without any member.
Permitted participants
Resident individuals and entities may trade in exchange traded currency derivatives only with underlying exposure limits for certain pairs, and FPIs have separate limits.
A trader without exposure is limited to a position cap.
Anyone may take unlimited positions.
Operating range
Exchanges set daily price bands to restrict extreme movements in contract prices.
An order outside the range is rejected.
There is no limit on daily price movement.
Price bands and circuit breakers
If prices move beyond set limits, trading can be paused to calm the market.
Trading halts after a sharp fall.
Circuit breakers apply only to equities.
Trade confirmation
Trades are confirmed through contract notes issued by the broker.
A client receives a contract note after execution.
Contract notes are issued monthly.
Client code modification
Modifying client codes after trade is restricted and subject to penalties, to prevent misuse.
A broker cannot change codes freely to shift trades.
Client codes can be changed any time.
Contracts on offer
Different currency pairs and expiry months are available, with near-month contracts typically being most liquid.
Near-month USD-INR futures see heavy trading.
Far-month contracts are the most liquid.

units.title: Clearing, settlement and risk management
units.overview: Margins, daily settlement and the guarantee of the clearing corporation.
facts: Clearing corporation
The clearing corporation acts as the counterparty to every trade, guaranteeing its performance.
The buyer and seller each deal with the clearing corporation.
Buyers and sellers deal directly with each other.
Initial margin
Initial margin is collected up front to cover the potential loss on a position over a short period.
A client deposits margin before taking a position.
Initial margin is returned immediately.
SPAN margin
SPAN margin is computed by a risk-based method that estimates the worst loss across scenarios for the portfolio.
The system calculates margin for combined positions.
SPAN margin is a fixed percentage of premium.
Extreme loss margin
An additional margin is collected to cover losses beyond the normal scenario.
A buffer margin is added for extreme moves.
Extreme loss margin replaces initial margin.
Mark-to-market settlement
Daily mark-to-market profits and losses are settled in cash through the clearing banks.
A losing member pays the loss the next morning.
Gains and losses are carried until expiry.
Daily settlement price
The daily settlement price is based on the weighted average price of the last half hour of trading.
Positions are marked at the daily settlement price.
The settlement price is the opening price.
Final settlement
At expiry open positions are settled in cash at the final settlement price and the contract ceases.
A position is closed automatically at expiry.
Open positions roll over automatically.
Margin call
If margin falls below the requirement, the member must top it up promptly or face position closure.
A client receives a call to add funds.
A margin call is a request to withdraw funds.
Option premium settlement
Option premiums are paid by the buyer and received by the seller on the next day after the trade.
A buyer pays the premium after the trade.
Premiums are paid at expiry.
Settlement guarantee fund
A fund maintained by the clearing corporation protects the market in the event of member default.
The fund helps to complete settlement in a default.
The fund pays clients' trading profits.
Position limits and risk
Position limits for members and clients help control concentration and systemic risk.
A member cannot hold positions above its cap.
Limits only apply to the exchange.
Default management
In a default, the clearing corporation closes positions, uses the defaulter's margin and then other resources as per a waterfall.
The defaulter's margin is used first.
The clearing corporation ignores defaults.

units.title: Regulatory framework
units.overview: The authorities and rules that govern currency derivatives.
facts: RBI role
The RBI regulates foreign exchange and the currency derivatives framework along with SEBI.
The RBI issues rules on forex and eligible participants.
The RBI has no role in currency derivatives.
SEBI role
SEBI regulates exchange-traded currency derivatives, including exchanges, brokers and trading rules.
SEBI approves contract specifications.
SEBI regulates only mutual funds.
FEMA
The Foreign Exchange Management Act governs foreign exchange transactions in India.
Cross-border payments follow FEMA rules.
FEMA is a tax law.
Underlying exposure
Residents may hold positions in some pairs freely, while in others positions beyond limits require proof of underlying exposure.
A trader with no exposure stays within the cap.
Exposure proof is never required.
Eligible pairs
Exchange traded contracts are available only in pairs permitted by the RBI and SEBI, including INR pairs and certain cross-currency pairs.
USD-INR and EUR-INR contracts are listed.
Any currency pair can be listed.
Position limits for clients
Limits for individual clients are set at a set dollar amount of gross open position per currency pair.
Retail position caps apply.
There are no client-level limits.
Broker obligations
Brokers must follow KYC, risk disclosure and record-keeping rules under SEBI and exchange regulations.
A broker gives the client a risk disclosure document.
Brokers may skip KYC for small clients.
Grievance redressal
Investors can approach the broker, then the exchange and SEBI to resolve complaints.
A client escalates an unresolved complaint to the exchange.
Clients cannot complain about brokers.

units.title: Accounting and taxation
units.overview: How gains from currency derivatives are treated for accounting and tax.
facts: Business income
Profits and losses from exchange traded currency derivatives are generally treated as non-speculative business income.
A trader reports gains as business income.
Gains are treated as capital gains.
Non-speculative loss
Non-speculative business losses can be set off against other income except salary, and carried forward for eight years.
A trader carries forward unabsorbed losses.
Business losses can never be carried forward.
Turnover for audit
Turnover from derivatives is computed on the basis of the absolute sum of profits and losses, with audit rules based on thresholds.
A trader calculates turnover for tax audit.
Turnover is the total contract value.
Accounting at settlement
Daily mark-to-market gains and losses are recognised in accounts on settlement or at the balance sheet date for open positions.
Unsettled positions are marked at year end.
Accounting ignores open positions.
Transaction costs
Brokerage, exchange charges, GST and stamp duty apply to currency derivative trades.
The contract note shows these charges.
There are no costs besides brokerage.
Record maintenance
Traders should maintain contract notes, margin statements and ledgers to substantiate returns.
A trader keeps statements for tax filing.
Records are not needed for tax filing.

units.title: Codes of conduct and investor protection
units.overview: Ethical duties of intermediaries and the safeguards for investors.
facts: Code of conduct
Intermediaries must act with integrity, diligence and fairness and avoid manipulative practices.
A broker refuses to execute a manipulative trade.
The code allows guaranteeing returns.
Risk disclosure
Brokers must inform clients of the risks, including leverage and potential losses beyond margin.
A client signs the risk disclosure form.
Disclosure is needed only for large clients.
Suitability and mis-selling
Products should match the client's needs and understanding, and mis-selling is a violation.
A dealer explains the risk of a short option.
A dealer may push complex products to all clients.
Front running
Trading ahead of a client's order for personal gain is prohibited.
A dealer trades before executing a client order.
Front running is acceptable on small orders.
Investor Protection Fund
The exchange maintains a fund to compensate investors in case of a broker default up to specified limits.
A client of a defaulting broker may claim compensation.
The fund covers market losses.
Confidentiality
Client data must be kept confidential and disclosed only as required by law.
A dealer does not share client positions.
Client positions may be shared with other clients.
Complaint resolution
Complaints should be acknowledged and resolved within prescribed timelines.
A firm responds to a complaint in time.
Complaints may be ignored.
